StreamEdit · Experiment R22 · 18 Aug 2026

Where quality arrives in a streaming edit

A metric surface over two axes — how much of the clip you have seen, and how far the sampler has run — for three blend-schedule arms on 22 FiVE-Bench clips. Two things fall out: the metrics stop moving at roughly half the sampler budget, and the arms differ sharply in how well the edit survives to the end of the clip.

Why the surface can be trusted

The last column is the real video, proven three ways

Every claim here rests on one identity: the step-14 column of the matrix has to be the arm's actual final output, not an approximation of it. That was closed at three levels before any figure was drawn.

L1 · latent

Assert inside the sampler

The dumped step-14 latent equals the returned rollout latent, asserted per window and again after the multi-window stitch.

L2 · pixel

Bit-identical renders

Step-14 PNGs match the stored R1 / R7 / R21 reference renders on 1482 of 1482 frames per arm — 4446 of 4446 in total, including the multi-window clip 0034_cows.

L3 · metric

Exact, not tolerant

M(n,14) equals the plain step-14 per-frame mean with max |diff| = 0.0 across all 528 (arm × clip × metric) cells.

Finding 1

The metrics stop moving at step 7–8 of 15

Each panel below shows the deviation of the running metric from its own final value, so the last column is white by construction and the eye reads convergence directly. Across every metric and every arm the field goes flat at j ≈ 7–8: the last seven denoising steps move the numbers by under one percent.

Median earliest step from which the full-clip prefix stays within 1% of its final value, over the 22 clips. Lower is earlier.

The split across the table is itself informative. Editing signal lands early — cos_third_pvp reaches its final clip-to-target score by step 6, four steps before either paper arm. Preservation metrics settle later — mse and structure_distance need 11 to 12 steps in every arm. Whatever the last third of the sampler is doing, it is refining background fidelity, not the edit.

This does not say "8 steps suffice"

Vj is each block's step-j prediction collected during one unperturbed 15-step rollout, where earlier blocks were already fully denoised and re-cached at clean context. It is a trajectory preview, not what a shortened sampler emits. The claim it supports is about where in the trajectory the editing signal lands; converting that into a compute saving requires an actual 8-step run.

Finding 2

The edit drifts away over the clip — unless the bank is persistent

Averaged over the bench, per-frame clip-to-target at step 14 falls from the first fifth of a clip to the last fifth by 1.02 points for paper_vp and 1.09 for paper_novp, while cos_third_pvp loses only 0.13. On individual clips the gap is far wider.

Per-frame clip-to-target at j=14, mean of the first 20% of frames versus the last 20%. Positive change means the edit strengthens across the clip.
Clipcos_third_pvppaper_vppaper_novp
0076_A_rabbit+1.57−3.56−3.62
0090_A_deer+2.66−1.18−0.32
0057_dog−1.29−0.82−1.75

The mosaics make the mechanism plain. Rows are pixel frames (every tenth), columns are denoising steps, so reading down the last column is watching the finished video play.

0076_A_rabbit

The edit is rabbit → drone. cos_third_pvp holds a clean, consistent drone in every frame from 0 to 80. paper_vp renders the drone only in frame 0 — the anchored frame — and from frame 10 onward it collapses into a shapeless pale blob that is neither rabbit nor drone. This is the clearest case of the persistent bank removing drift outright.

0090_A_deer

Same pattern, less extreme: cos_third_pvp strengthens across the clip (+2.66), while both paper arms sag in the middle and recover only partially by the end.

0057_dog

The honest counterexample. On the metric, paper_vp drifts least here (−0.82 against cos_third_pvp's −1.29) and sits higher in absolute terms. Visually cos_third_pvp still holds the robot-dog identity across all 57 frames, so this is a scoring difference rather than a collapse — but it does mean the persistent bank is not uniformly better.

Background drift is not fixed

LPIPS on the unedited region worsens across the clip by a similar amount in every arm (+0.10 rabbit, +0.07 deer, +0.15 dog for cos_third_pvp, within 0.03 of the paper arms). The persistent bank preserves the edit; it does not stop the background from degrading. Consistent with the absolute-value figures, where cos_third_pvp sits at visibly higher LPIPS than paper_vp throughout.

Reading limits

What would change these conclusions

  1. Deviation is largest at small prefixes, not at the full clip. Mean |D| in the first 20% of frames runs 1.4–1.6 CLIP points against 0.9–1.0 at the whole clip, and the same ordering holds for every metric. That is an averaging artefact of the cumulative mean — few frames early, heavily damped late — not evidence about drift. Drift has to be read from per-frame values, which is what Finding 2 uses.

  2. M(i,j) is a cumulative prefix mean, not the metric at frame i. Movement along the row axis is damped and dominated by early frames.

  3. 22 clips, edit types 1/2/5/6. Full-bench numbers for these arms live in R21; treat everything here as corroboration on a subset, not an independent measurement.

  4. One clip contradicts the drift story on the metric (0057_dog), and the three mosaic clips were chosen to illustrate the effect, not sampled at random. The bench-wide averages in Finding 2 are the unbiased statement; the mosaics are the mechanism.

  5. clip_similarity_source_image is a null control. It scores the source video, so it is constant along j and renders flat by construction — its invariance across all 45 evaluation runs also confirms harness determinism.
